00_missingness.title: Missing values over time
00_missingness.caption: Delhi's CPCB record is nearly complete: PM2.5 is missing on 2 days. Gaps cluster in a 2017 outage for PM10, SO2 and O3. Xylene (39% missing) is not used.

01_pm25_timeseries.title: Delhi PM2.5, 2015 to mid-2020
01_pm25_timeseries.caption: A spike starts in every 15 Oct to 30 Nov window (shaded), with peaks up to 685 µg/m³. Levels stay high into Dec and Jan, after the fires stop, so weather alone produces severe smog.

02_monthly_box.title: Seasonality
02_monthly_box.caption: Monthly medians run from 43 (Aug, monsoon) to 210 µg/m³ (Nov–Dec). The seasonal-mean baseline shows what the calendar alone explains.

03_fires_vs_pm25.title: Fires and PM2.5 together
03_fires_vs_pm25.caption: 69% of Punjab and Haryana fire detections fall in 15 Oct to 30 Nov. The April–May wheat fires produce no PM2.5 spike: summer weather disperses the smoke.

04_fire_map.title: Where the fires are
04_fire_map.caption: The bounding box captures 92% of Oct–Nov detections in the wider window. It is approximate and includes a sliver of western UP.

05_lag_correlation.title: Which fire lags matter?
05_lag_correlation.caption: Within Oct–Nov, the fire to PM2.5 correlation rises from 0.27 (same day) to 0.48 (4–5 days), so 3- and 7-day rolling fire sums are used.

06_weather_vs_pm25.title: Weather confounders
06_weather_vs_pm25.caption: Calm air (wind, ρ = −0.34) and a shallow mixing layer (ρ = −0.44) trap pollution. These conditions coincide with the burning season, so the fair comparison must include weather.

07_wind_direction.title: Wind direction on bad days
07_wind_direction.caption: NW winds (from Punjab) dominate the cool season on all days. Severe days are not more often NW, so direction alone is not the mechanism.

08_corr_heatmap.title: Feature correlations
08_corr_heatmap.caption: Tomorrow's PM2.5 correlates 0.90 with today's. Fire features correlate 0.44–0.54, but they are confounded with temperature and season.

09_diwali.title: Diwali inside the burning season
09_diwali.caption: PM2.5 jumps the day after Diwali (2017: 176 → 427). A Diwali flag is in both model variants so fireworks aren't credited to fires.

R1_model_comparison.title: Model comparison, 2019 test year
R1_model_comparison.caption: Tree models beat persistence overall and in the burning season. The seasonal mean is far worse: yesterday's air matters more than the calendar.

R2_test_season_forecast.title: 2019 season: observed vs forecasts
R2_test_season_forecast.caption: Forecasts follow reality with about a one-day lag. They gain mainly by not over-shooting after a peak collapses.

R3_bootstrap.title: Bootstrap of the 2019 fire effect
R3_bootstrap.caption: On 2019 alone, fires cut Random Forest error by 4.5%. The 95% CI just touches zero.

R4_error_analysis.title: Error analysis
R4_error_analysis.caption: Systematic shrinkage: clean days are over-predicted (+12) and Severe days under-predicted (−70). The largest bias is in Dec–Jan.

R5_permutation_importance.title: Permutation importance
R5_permutation_importance.caption: Today's PM2.5 dominates. Individual fire features look negligible because they stand in for each other.

R6_partial_dependence.title: Partial dependence on recent fires
R6_partial_dependence.caption: The model's response to fires is larger with NW wind (+17 vs +6 µg/m³): plausible transport, but within the noise (see R8).

R7_ridge_coefficients.title: Ridge coefficients
R7_ridge_coefficients.caption: Standardised effects on log PM2.5: persistence, season, humidity, temperature and wind come first.

R8_robustness_fire_gain.title: Robustness: three seasons × three horizons
R8_robustness_fire_gain.caption: Single-season fire gains swing from −19% to +8%. Pooled over 2017–19, every 95% CI includes zero, so the 2019 gain does not generalise.

R9_error_vs_horizon.title: Error vs forecast horizon
R9_error_vs_horizon.caption: The models' edge over persistence grows from 7% (1 day) to 14% (3 days). The with-fires and without-fires lines coincide.
